findings.claim: When a retro's data-gathering surfaces that Sprint estimates felt off, anchoring — not poor skill — is often the explanatory frame.

findings.claim: Most retro practices — standups, velocity tracking, pair programming, code review ratios — lack controlled-experiment support.

findings.claim: Standard deviation of LOC estimates is approximately one-quarter of the mean.

findings.fix: correct: **Implementations of the same specification vary in size by about a quarter of the mean.**

findings.claim: the visible defects are a fraction of the latent mistake population; count-based metrics systematically undercount the problem space.
findings.failure_mode: Inference runs against the deep ref's conclusion. Jones's point is that mistakes that never produce a fault experience are not worth the cost of finding; the distillation recasts them as an undercounted 'problem space'.
findings.evidence: Deep 171: 'many coding mistakes never produce a fault experience and the cost of finding and fixing them all is wasted.'
findings.fix: correct: ... the latent mistakes that never fire are not a backlog to chase; Jones's point is that finding and fixing them all is wasted cost.

findings.claim: retrospective data from past Sprints that was never written down or is scattered across tools is not a team-laziness problem but follows the same decay curve.
findings.failure_mode: Figure transferred to the wrong population: the 17%/year is the availability of research datasets (Vines et al.), not team memory or sprint records.
findings.fix: strip the application, or keep only the finding: research datasets become unavailable at about 17% per year, which is why Jones urges keeping data.

findings.claim: Are the coding mistakes that are producing fault experiences concentrated on a small set of high-frequency input paths (the bi-exponential pattern)?
findings.failure_mode: Jones's explanation of the bi-exponential is 'speculative'; the input-path concentration mechanism is not in the deep ref.
findings.fix: correct: Are a few faults being experienced far more often than the rest (the bi-exponential pattern of repeat fault reports)?

findings.claim: What range of improvement is realistic given the corrected 6:1 spread? Is the target within the empirical range of individual-developer variation
findings.failure_mode: Category error: the Grant-Sackman correction is a between-developer spread, not a bound on how much a team can improve.
findings.fix: correct: Does the target rest on an assumed between-developer spread (28:1) that the evidence corrects to 14:1 at most and 6:1 or less once batch/time-sharing is separated out?

findings.claim: Anchoring to a stakeholder or manager figure is the more likely explanation than poor skill
